summary: Teach 10-11 year olds to calculate the mean (add the values, divide by the count) AND interpret it as the fair-share/levelling value: what each data point would be if the total were shared equally. The central aim is to prevent the mean becoming an empty procedure. Build it as levelling/fair share (evening out towers of cubes to a common height) alongside the algorithm, then use two revealing non-transparent tasks — the reverse problem (find a missing value using total = mean \u00d7 count) and reasoning about how adding a value (including 0) shifts the mean. Reinforce the properties that let children sanity-check: the mean lies between the lowest and highest values, is influenced by every value, and need not equal any actual data value.
misconceptions: Knowing only the add-and-divide rule with no sense of what the mean represents, so any non-standard problem fails
Believing that adding a data value of 0 does not change the mean (not seeing that the mean is influenced by every value and that the count also rises)
Being unable to find a missing value given the mean — re-averaging the known values instead of using total = mean × count
Expecting the mean to equal one of the data values, or placing it outside the range of the data
Dividing by the wrong count (e.g. ignoring a zero or a repeated value when counting the data points)

activities.title: Level the towers: the mean as fair share
steps: Start with five towers of cubes at different heights (e.g. representing scores), choosing heights whose total is a multiple of 5 so whole cubes can be shared equally, and even them out by moving cubes from the tall towers onto the short ones until every tower is the same height.
State that this common height IS the mean — what each would be if the total were shared equally.
Compute sum \u00f7 count and confirm it equals the levelled height, so the fair-share meaning and the rule are seen as the same thing.
Answer 'if all five pupils had scored the same, what would each have scored?' and 'what does this mean value tell us about the scores?'
activities.insight: The mean is the value every data point would share if the total were distributed equally; the add-and-divide algorithm computes exactly this fair share, so the rule has a meaning rather than being an arbitrary procedure.

activities.title: The reverse problem: find the missing value
steps: Given a mean and all-but-one of the values (e.g. four of five spelling scores were 7, 9, 6 and 10; the mean of all five is 8), find the missing value.
Reconstruct the total using total = mean \u00d7 count (8 \u00d7 5 = 40), subtract the known values (40 \u2212 32 = 8) to recover the missing one.
Explain why re-averaging only the known four values is wrong — the mean refers to all five.
activities.insight: Because the mean is the total shared equally, the total is fixed at mean \u00d7 count; recovering a missing value means finding that total and subtracting what is known, not re-averaging the visible data.

activities.title: Does a zero change the mean?
steps: Start from a stated data set of positive test scores with a known mean (e.g. 72, 85, 90, 68, 95 with mean 82), predict what happens to the mean when a new value of 0 is added, then recompute to check.
Notice that both the total and the count change (here from 5 values to 6), and that the new 0 still counts as a data point.

State that, because the existing scores are positive, the current mean is positive, so the added 0 lies below it: the mean goes DOWN (e.g. 410 \u00f7 6 \u2248 68.3), pulled toward zero as part of the fair share.
Extend to an extreme value: predict then compute the effect of adding one more score of 100 to the stated set (which, being above the current mean, pulls the mean up).
activities.insight: Every value — including 0 — influences the mean, and adding a data point also increases the count; for positive scores an added 0 sits below the current mean and lowers it, so it does not leave the mean unchanged.

activities.title: Properties of the mean: sanity-checking an answer
steps: For a data set with its mean marked, confirm the mean lies between the lowest and highest values and check it is not greater than every score nor less than every score.
Point out a case where the mean equals none of the actual values (e.g. nobody scored 82, yet 82 is the mean) and explain why that is fine.
Given a computed mean, judge whether it is plausible by checking it falls within the data range.
Answer the counterexample 'could the mean ever be higher than every single score? Why or why not?'
activities.insight: The mean always lies between the lowest and highest values (inclusive) and need not equal any actual data value (it can even be a fraction with no physical counterpart), so a mean outside the data range signals a computation error.

activities.title: Scorable practice and self-check
steps: Compute the mean of a small clean data set (fill-in-the-blank).
Solve a reverse item: 'four of five scores are…; the mean is 8; find the fifth.'
Answer a multiple-choice item: 'a new pupil scores 0 — does the mean go up, down, or stay the same?' (for a set of positive scores).
Spot an implausible mean: choose which proposed mean cannot be right because it falls outside the data range.
activities.insight: Calculating, interpreting, reversing and sanity-checking the mean can each be checked against a correct answer, catching the zero and missing-value errors.

checkQuestion: Set these tasks and WATCH how the child works, saying little. (1) 'Here are five test scores: 72, 85, 90, 68, 95. Work out the mean, and tell me what that number tells us about the scores.' (2) A reverse task: 'Four of five spelling scores were 7, 9, 6 and 10. The mean of all five was 8. What was the fifth score?' (3) 'A new pupil then scored 0 on the spelling test. Does the mean go up, down, or stay the same? Work it out.' (Set the task and WATCH — do not hint at total = mean × count or at what happens with the zero.)
checkAnswer: A correct performance: for (1) sums to 410 and divides by 5 to get 82, and describes 82 as a typical / fair-share score that need not equal any actual score; for (2) uses total = mean × count (8×5 = 40), subtracts the known 32, giving 8 — not re-averaging the four; for (3) recomputes and states the mean goes DOWN because the 0 counts and pulls it toward zero (the count also rises). Solving the reverse problem and reasoning correctly about the zero are the marks of conceptual mastery.
